messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Raj, a 40‑year‑old South‑Eastern Asian journalist, was captured in the turmoil that swept his hometown three years ago. He had been on assignment in a rebel‑occupied district when an armed unit detained him, and the interrogation that followed was a brutal mix of physical torture and psychological humiliation. The soldiers stripped him of his identity, bound him to a chair, and repeatedly forced him to answer questions that violated his professional code, demanding that he reveal confidential sources. When the beating intensified, the guards used a child’s crying as a tool of terror, holding a baby’s recorded sobs over his head while he lay helpless. The torture ended when he was left bruised and delirious, the memory of the event still flickering like a broken film reel. From that night onward, the very sound of children crying, the sudden dizziness that accompanies his own internal “names” when he hears a colleague’s voice, and hearing the names of those he had once trusted as a journalist, have become unrelenting triggers. When a distant cry of a child reaches his ears, it sets off a cascade: it triggers his avoidance of social contacts, heightens his startle reactions, dredges up the fragmented memory, and fuels his belief that others can see what happened to him. The sudden dizziness he feels when a familiar name surfaces propels him to scan the room for potential threats, leading him to watch others closely for any sign that they might harm him. The echo of those names also stirs the memory gaps that still haunt him, as if each syllable could unlock a forgotten part of the night. These triggers reinforce his negative appraisals, as he comes to believe that he is defective and that his past actions violated his own values. His negative appraisals, in turn, deepen the cycle. Feeling exposed, Raj sees his colleagues and friends as potential judges, and this belief spurs him to avoid any social contact, even at work. The sense of being defective pushes him to dwell on how the event could have been prevented, a rumination that keeps his mind tethered to the past. He also watches people in the newsroom with a heightened suspicion, convinced that any smile might mask a threat. Each negative emotion—fear, guilt, shame—ignores the quiet moments he might otherwise have allowed for healing, turning the memory of the torture into a living, breathing threat that refuses to let him rest. The memory of the night, fragmented though it may be, also fuels the maladaptive strategies he has adopted. When he struggles to recall the details, he finds himself avoiding any situation that might force him to relive the experience, and he restricts his food intake to the point where he is constantly hungry yet refuses to eat. The startle to ordinary sounds—his phone ringing, a siren in the distance—continues to keep his body on edge, while the knowledge that he might again be seen as defective keeps him from speaking out about the injustice he endured. In his avoidance, Raj has begun to withdraw from the very people who once trusted him; his partner left him after a heated argument about his inability to share his pain. He has also started to doubt the very core of his identity as a journalist committed to truth, feeling that his suffering has betrayed those principles. As weeks became months, the cycle tightened. The auditory cue of a child’s cry in a newsroom break room now brings a sudden dizziness, which in turn forces him to flee the staff lounge and return home. In the quiet of his apartment, he watches television programs about crime, and each clip of a potential threat triggers a flurry of negative emotions that spiral into rumination. He continues to avoid meals, feeling that each bite might betray the self he has always claimed to be. He stops attending the weekly writer’s group, fearing that hearing the laughter of others would reveal his vulnerability. Raj’s body aches from the constant tension, and he finds himself unable to recall the exact sequence of the torture, but he knows that each memory fragment is as real as the present day. Now, after a month of escalating anxiety and the loss of his regular beat assignment due to missed deadlines, Raj finally stepped into a therapist’s office. He came in feeling that his life had become a series of loops—each trigger spiraling into avoidance, each avoidance feeding the fear of being seen, each fear fueling more avoidance, and so on. He is most afraid that his journalistic career will dissolve into silence, and he hopes that by confronting these triggers and the negative appraisals they ignite, he can reclaim the sense of control that has been lost for years.
